absent: No critical AI scholarship (no Bender, Crawford or epistemic-injustice work), no philosophy of technology behind the 'epistemic agent' claim, and no connectivism critics beyond Kop & Hill.
forYou: The pre-AI layer is the interesting part for Professional Criticality: strip the model out and stages 1, 2 and 4 are inquiry, source criticism and knowledge circulation. Bovill's co-creation is also the bridge to your participatory work.
method: References read from the article; strands and narrative by Claude, grounded only in those citations.
narrative: The root is Siemens (2005): learning as forming and traversing connections, with knowledge residing partly in non-human nodes. Kop and Hill (2008) appear as the early assessment of that claim.

Around it sits a pre-AI pedagogy layer — student-generated questions (Chin & Brown 2002; Aflalo 2021), critical reflection (Mezirow 1998; Ash & Clayton 2009; Helyer 2015) and simulation-based training (Bell et al. 2008). The four stages are largely this tradition, re-sequenced around a model.

The co-creation vocabulary comes from Bovill (2016, 2020), whose concern is redistributing power between students and staff. The rest of the citations are 2023-2026 AI-in-education papers, including Draxler et al. (2024) on AI ghostwriting, which anchors the epistemic-ownership avenue.
